entry: Country in West Asia, at the head of the [[Persian Gulf]] on the northeastern edge of the Arabian Peninsula. It borders [[Iraq]] to the north and [[Saudi Arabia]] to the south. As of 2024, the population was 4.82 million, of whom 1.53 million were citizens; most residents live in the metropolitan area of [[Kuwait City]], the capital. A British protectorate from 1899, Kuwait became independent in June 1961. Oil was discovered in 1938, and oil income financed rapid modernization from 1946 to 1982. In 1990, Ba'athist Iraq invaded and annexed the country under [[Saddam Hussein]]. The occupation ended on February 26, 1991, after a U.S.-led coalition expelled Iraqi forces during the [[Gulf War]]. Kuwait is a high-income economy with the world's sixth-largest oil reserves. The Al Sabah family dominates politics under an emir. It is a member of the [[United Nations]] and [[OPEC]].

Capital and largest city of [[Kuwait]], on the south shore of Kuwait Bay on the [[Persian Gulf]]. It is the political, cultural and economic center of the country, home to most Kuwaiti corporations and the entire banking system. As of 2018, the metropolitan area had roughly three million inhabitants, more than 70% of the national population. A fishing village in the early 1700s, it was settled by the Bani Utub in the mid-1700s and became a trading hub between India, Muscat, [[Baghdad]] and Arabia. Boat-building and maritime trade expanded during the Persian siege of Basra (1775–1779), and the [[East India Company]] began using the port in 1792. During the reign of Mubarak Al-Sabah it was called the "[[Marseille]] of the Gulf". Today Kuwait International Airport and the Shuwaikh and Ahmadi ports serve its trade and transport.

Province of [[South Africa]] on the Indian Ocean coast, created in 1994 by merging the Zulu bantustan of KwaZulu with Natal Province. Its capital is Pietermaritzburg and its largest city is [[Durban]], home to the largest port in sub-Saharan Africa. It borders [[Mozambique]], [[Eswatini]] and [[Lesotho]]. The iSimangaliso Wetland Park and the uKhahlamba Drakensberg Park are [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Sites. The Zulu Kingdom remained independent until 1879. Albert Luthuli, the 1960 Nobel Peace Prize laureate, and Pixley ka Isaka Seme, founder of the [[African National Congress]], were born here.

Ghanaian politician and Pan-Africanist, first prime minister and then president of [[Ghana]] (1957–1966). As leader of the Convention People's Party, he led the Gold Coast to independence from the United Kingdom in 1957, a first in sub-Saharan Africa at the time. His government was [[Socialism|socialist]] and nationalist, funding industrial and energy projects and expanding education. A founding member of the Organization of African Unity, he promoted continental unity. He won the Lenin Peace Prize in 1962. After a 1964 amendment made Ghana a one-party state, he repressed opposition and was president for life. He was overthrown in a 1966 coup by the National Liberation Council. Complicity by the [[Central Intelligence Agency]] has been claimed but never fully verified. He spent the rest of his life in [[Guinea]], where he was named honorary co-president.

Annual African-American celebration held from December 26 to January 1, culminating in a communal feast called Karamu. Activist Maulana Karenga created it in 1966, drawing on African harvest festivals. Each of its seven days honors one of the Nguzo Saba, or seven principles. The name derives from the [[Swahili]] phrase matunda ya kwanza, meaning "first fruits". Karenga first framed it as an alternative to [[Christmas]], though many celebrants also observe Christmas. A 2009 estimate placed the number of Americans who celebrate it between 500,000 and 2,000,000.

Capital and largest city of [[Ukraine]] (pop., 2022: 2,952,301), straddling both banks of the [[Dnieper]] River. It is an industrial, scientific and cultural center with higher education institutions and an extensive transit system, including the Kyiv Metro. Its name is said to derive from Kyi, one of four legendary founders. A Slavic settlement on the trade route between Scandinavia and [[Constantinople]], it was a tributary of the Khazars until Varangians (Vikings) captured it in the mid-9th century. As capital of [[Kievan Rus']], the first East Slavic state, it was left in ruins by the Siege of Kiev in 1240. In 1918 the Ukrainian People's Republic declared independence from the Russian Republic after the [[October Revolution]], and Kyiv became its capital. It became capital of the Ukrainian SSR in 1934, within the [[Soviet Union]]. After Ukrainian independence in 1991, Kyiv remained the country's largest and wealthiest city.

American actor best known for his work with director [[David Lynch]]. He studied acting at the University of Washington, graduating in 1982. He played Dale Cooper in *Twin Peaks* (1990–1991 and the 2017 revival), winning a Golden Globe, and appeared as Paul Atreides in *Dune* (1984) and Jeffrey Beaumont in *Blue Velvet* (1986). Later television roles include *Sex and the City* (2000–2002) and *Desperate Housewives* (2006–2012). He voiced Riley's father in [[Pixar]]'s *Inside Out* (2015) and its 2024 sequel.

French footballer and captain of the France national team, playing as a forward for Real Madrid. He began his senior career with Monaco and won the 2016–17 [[Ligue 1]] title before joining Paris Saint-Germain in 2017. He won 15 trophies there, including six league titles, and joined Real Madrid in 2024. At the 2018 [[FIFA World Cup]] he became the second teenager, after [[Pelé]], to score in a World Cup final and win the tournament. He holds the record for most goals in World Cup finals, with four.

Australian singer, songwriter and actress, often called the "Princess of Pop." Born and raised in [[Melbourne]], she first gained fame in the soap opera *Neighbours*. She began a music career in the late 1980s, and her 2001 single "Can't Get You Out of My Head" was a worldwide chart-topper. Her album *Fever* (2001) is her best-selling to date, and she has won two [[Grammy Awards]], four Brit Awards and 18 ARIA Music Awards. Her sales exceed 80 million records, the most by any Australian-born female artist. In 2024, [[Time (magazine)|Time]] named her one of the 100 most influential people.

City, capital of Kyoto Prefecture in the Kansai region of [[Japan]] (pop., 2020: 1.46 million). Emperor Kanmu chose it as the imperial capital in 794, and emperors ruled there until 1869. Its original name, Heian-kyō, was modeled on the [[Tang dynasty]] capital Chang'an. It was the scene of key events in the Sengoku period and the [[Boshin War]], and the capital moved to [[Tokyo]] after the Meiji Restoration. Kyoto was spared large-scale destruction in [[World War II]], so much of its prewar heritage survives. It is considered Japan's cultural capital, with numerous Buddhist temples, Shinto shrines, palaces and gardens, some designated a World Heritage Site by [[UNESCO]]. Landmarks include the Kyoto Imperial Palace, Kiyomizu-dera and Kinkaku-ji; the video game company [[Nintendo]] is based in the city. It is also a center of higher learning, including [[Kyoto University]], the second-oldest university in Japan.

National research university in [[Kyoto]], Japan. Founded as Kyoto Imperial University in 1897, it is the second-oldest university in Japan after the [[University of Tokyo]]. Its roots lie in a Chemistry School founded in Osaka in 1869, and it was financed with reparations from the [[First Sino-Japanese War]]. It dropped "Imperial" from its name in 1947 under Allied Occupation reforms. It has 10 undergraduate faculties, 18 graduate schools and 13 research institutes, across three main campuses in Kyoto. It is said that the motto "freedom of academic culture" originated with law professor Yoshihito Takane. The library network holds more than 7.49 million books, the second-largest university library in Japan. As of 2024, it counts 21 [[Nobel Prize]] laureates among its alumni and faculty, and two [[Fields Medal|Fields Medalists]].

Landlocked, mountainous country in [[Central Asia]], formerly known as Kirghizia. Its capital and largest city is [[Bishkek]], on the northern border with [[Kazakhstan]]. Ethnic Kyrgyz make up most of its 7.5 million people, with Uzbek and Russian minorities. The [[Mongol Empire]] conquered it in the 13th century, and the region was later invaded by the Dzungar Khanate. In 1876 it became part of the [[Russian Empire]], and in 1936 it became a republic of the [[Soviet Union]]. It declared independence on August 31, 1991. It has been a presidential, parliamentary and semi-presidential republic at different times, reverting to a presidential system in 2021. The transition economy relies on re-exporting Chinese goods and gold production, and the country is ranked 117th in the [[Human Development Index]]. It joined the [[World Trade Organization]] in 1998.

Third-largest and most southerly of the four main islands of [[Japan]]. Its name derives from nine ancient provinces on the island. It covers 36,782 sq km and had a population of 12,382,121 in 2025, similar to that of [[New Guinea]] or [[Cuba]]. It is separated from [[Honshu]] by the Kanmon Straits. Mount Aso, Japan's largest active [[Volcano|volcano]], rises to 1,591 m (5,220 ft) in central Kyushu. Numerous [[Hot spring|hot springs]] at Beppu and around Mount Aso reflect its tectonic activity. Major crops include rice, tea, tobacco and sweet potatoes, and silk is widely produced. Its population clusters in the northwest, around [[Fukuoka]] and Kitakyushu. Politically, it is a stronghold of the [[Liberal Democratic Party (Japan)|Liberal Democratic Party]].

Sexual and gender minorities, including [[Lesbian|lesbian]], [[Gay men|gay]], bisexual, [[Transgender|transgender]] and queer people. The group is often extended to include questioning, [[Intersex|intersex]], asexual, pansexual, aromantic and agender people. Its members have a broad range of [[Sexual orientation|sexual orientations]] and gender identities. Variants of the initialism include LGBT+, LGBTQIA+ and QUILTBAG. Community life includes Pride events, LGBTQ social venues and, in some places, gay villages. Culture includes Pride parades and events such as the Gay Games, although not all LGBTQ people identify with it. The Queercore and Gay Shame movements criticize what they see as the commercialization of LGBTQ culture. Same-sex love and gender variance are documented across premodern and modern cultures, but many societies have marginalized and persecuted such people. LGBT History Month began in the United States in 1994.

American rapper and actor, one of the earliest rappers to achieve crossover commercial success alongside [[Run-DMC]]. Signed to Def Jam Recordings in 1984, he broke through with "I Need a Beat" and released *Radio* in 1985. His albums include *Mama Said Knock You Out* (1990) and *Mr. Smith* (1995), and he is a two-time Grammy Award winner. From 2009 to 2023 he played Sam Hanna on the [[CBS]] series *NCIS: Los Angeles*. In 2017 he became the first rapper to receive the Kennedy Center Honors, and in 2021 he joined the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]].

Public research university in [[Munich]], [[Bavaria]], Germany. Founded as the University of Ingolstadt in 1472, it is the sixth-oldest university in Germany in continuous operation. It moved to Landshut in 1800 during the [[Napoleonic Wars]], then to Munich in 1826, and was renamed Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität in 1802. The university is organized in 18 faculties, including theology, law, medicine, physics and psychology. With 52,658 matriculated students in the 2025/26 winter semester, it is Germany's second-largest university by enrollment and its largest on-site. As of 2023 it is associated with 50 Nobel laureates, including faculty and alumni such as [[Pope Benedict XVI]], [[Richard Strauss]], [[Wolfgang Pauli]] and [[Bertolt Brecht]]. It holds the title "University of Excellence" under the German Universities Excellence Initiative and is a member of U15 and LERU. In 2024 it recorded 879.0 million [[Euro|euros]] in funding, excluding the university hospital.

Semisynthetic psychedelic drug derived from [[Ergot|ergot]]. Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) acts mainly on [[Serotonin|serotonin]] receptors. No fatal human overdoses have been documented. Albert Hofmann synthesized it in 1938 and discovered its effects in 1943. It was used experimentally in psychiatry in the 1950s and 1960s to treat [[Alcoholism|alcoholism]] and [[Schizophrenia|schizophrenia]]. By the mid-1960s it was central to the counterculture in [[San Francisco]] and [[London]]. The [[United States]] classified it as a Schedule I drug in 1970; the [[United Nations]] followed in 1971. In 2024 the Food and Drug Administration designated it a breakthrough therapy for generalized anxiety disorder.

French luxury goods [[Conglomerate (company)|conglomerate]] headquartered in Paris. Formed in 1987 through the merger of Louis Vuitton and Moët Hennessy, it controls about 60 subsidiaries with 75 luxury brands. They include Christian Dior, Givenchy, Fendi, Tiffany & Co. and Bulgari. [[Bernard Arnault]] is its chairman, chief executive and largest shareholder. In April 2023 it became the first European company to be valued at more than $500 billion. In 2023 it was ranked 47th in the [[Forbes]] Global 2000. Its chief markets are France, Japan and the United States.

Mathematical theorem for evaluating limits of quotients of two functions. It applies to the indeterminate forms 0/0 and ∞/∞, where both functions tend to zero or both to infinity, and it replaces each function with its [[Derivative|derivative]]. The rule is named after the 17th-century French mathematician Guillaume de l'Hôpital, who published it in his 1696 textbook. The Swiss mathematician [[Johann Bernoulli]] discovered the result and sent it to l'Hôpital under a paid arrangement. The original result was later extended to other indeterminate forms.

Vietnamese rebel leader and founding emperor of the [[Lê dynasty|Later Lê dynasty]]. The [[Ming dynasty]] had conquered Đại Việt in 1406, after invading under the pretext of restoring the [[Trần dynasty]]. In 1418 Lê Lợi rose against Ming rule, using guerrilla tactics, constantly moving his camps and ambushing larger Ming forces. By 1427 his resistance had driven the Ming armies out of Vietnam and restored independence. After the victory he took the temple name Lê Thái Tổ and became the first monarch of the restored kingdom. He is often considered one of Vietnam's greatest national heroes. Born into a noble family in Thanh Hóa province, he was the youngest of three sons.

American writer and founder of [[Scientology]]. He wrote pulp science fiction and fantasy before publishing *Dianetics: The Modern Science of Mental Health* in 1950. He created Scientology in 1952 after losing the rights to Dianetics in bankruptcy. The church, variously described as a [[Cult|cult]], a [[New religious movement|new religious movement]] or a business, was led by Hubbard until his death. He briefly commanded two ships in [[World War II]] and was removed from command both times. In 1978 he was convicted of fraud in absentia in France, and 11 high-ranking members were indicted for espionage against the United States.

Longest-ruling Vietnamese imperial dynasty, from 1428 to 1789. Founded by [[Lê Lợi]] after he drove out the [[Ming dynasty]], it is also called the Later Lê dynasty. Its Initial Lê period (1428–1527) ended when the Mạc dynasty usurped the throne. In the Revival Lê period (1533–1789) emperors were figureheads under the Trịnh lords, amid the Lê–Mạc War and the Trịnh–Nguyễn Wars. The dynasty peaked under Lê Thánh Tông and declined after his death in 1497. Its southward expansion brought [[Champa]] under domination and reached into [[Laos]] and Myanmar. After 20 years of Ming rule, the state became Confucian, with a [[Civil service|civil service]] and laws modeled on China's. Western Europeans and Christianity arrived in the early 16th century. The Tây Sơn brothers ended the dynasty in 1789 by defeating both the Trịnh and the Nguyễn.

Sixth-largest of the [[Hawaiian Islands]], nicknamed the Pineapple Island for its former plantations. It is 98% owned by [[Larry Ellison]], co-founder and chairman of [[Oracle Corporation]]; the remainder belongs to the state of Hawaii or individual homeowners. It has a land area of 364 sq km (140.5 sq mi) and a population of 3,367 at the 2020 census. Nearby [[Maui]] controlled it from before recorded history, and its first settlers raised [[Taro|taro]]. Sugar cultivation in Hawaii began here in 1802. Lānaʻi has no traffic lights, and many landmarks are reachable only by four-wheel-drive dirt roads.

French physicist, inventor of the [[Foucault pendulum]]. In 1851 he demonstrated Earth's rotation with a pendulum suspended from the Panthéon in [[Paris]], and copies appeared in cities across Europe and America. He first worked to improve the photographic processes of [[Louis Daguerre]] and studied light with Hippolyte Fizeau. In 1850 he used a rotating mirror to measure the [[Speed of light|speed of light]], which he found slower in water than in air. He named the [[Gyroscope|gyroscope]] and discovered [[Eddy current|eddy currents]]. In 1857 he invented a polarizer bearing his name, and in 1858 he devised a method for testing reflecting telescope mirrors. He became physicist at the Paris Observatory in 1855 and received the Copley Medal the same year.

Senegalese poet, cultural theorist and politician, first president of [[Senegal]] from 1960 to 1980. A leading theorist of Négritude, he promoted African culture, black identity and African empowerment within French-African ties. He advocated full civil and political rights for France's African territories, arguing that French Africans would be better off in a federal French structure than as independent states. Senegal became independent in 1960 after a brief federation with [[Mali]]. After arresting prime minister Mamadou Dia on suspicion of plotting a coup in 1962, he established an authoritarian one-party state. In 1976 he permitted opposition parties but kept an unequal playing field, and he retired in 1980, handing power to Abdou Diouf. He founded the Senegalese Democratic Bloc in 1948 and was the first African elected to the Académie française.
